content: Ainhum is a condition characterized by a painful constriction at the base of the fifth toe, which often leads to spontaneous amputation (autoamputation) of the toe after several years. This condition is sometimes associated with palmoplantar keratoderma, although its exact cause remains unknown. The disease was first identified and described in detail by J.F. da Silva Lima in 1867. He observed it among the Nagos tribe in Bahia, Brazil, who referred to the condition as ainhum, meaning to saw, reflecting the painful loss of the fifth toe. The term is believed to have African origins, as the Nagos were linked to a native tribe in Nigeria through the transatlantic slave trade. Ainhum predominantly affects individuals of African descent, particularly those living in West Africa, South America, and India. It has also been reported in African American populations in the United States, with a prevalence of 2-7% in some studies. Cases in Europe are rare. The condition typically occurs in individuals aged 20 to 50, with an average age of onset around 38 years. The youngest reported case involved a seven-year-old child. There is no significant gender predilection. The exact etiology and pathogenesis of ainhum remain unclear. It is not caused by infections (parasitic, fungal, bacterial, or viral) or trauma. While walking barefoot during childhood has been suggested as a potential risk factor, the condition also occurs in individuals who have never walked barefoot. Race appears to be a significant predisposing factor, and there may be a genetic component, as familial cases have been reported. Some researchers, such as Dent et al., have proposed a genetically determined abnormality in the blood supply to the foot. Angiographic studies in affected limbs have shown attenuation of the posterior tibial artery at the ankle, absence of the plantar arch and its branches, and reliance on the dorsalis pedis artery for blood supply to the forefoot and little toe. Clinically, the disease begins with the formation of a groove on the lower and internal side of the base of the fifth toe, typically along the plantar-digital fold. This groove gradually deepens and becomes more circular. The progression rate varies, with some cases completing a full circle within months, while others remain incomplete for years. Approximately 75% of cases involve both feet, though the severity is often asymmetrical. The condition almost exclusively affects the fifth toe, although grooves have occasionally been observed on the fourth or third toes. The distal part of the affected toe swells, resembling a small potato, due to lymphatic edema distal to the constriction. Over time, crusts may form in the groove, which can become infected with Staphylococcus bacteria. As the groove deepens, it compresses tendons, blood vessels, and nerves. Bone resorption occurs due to pressure, without evidence of infection. Eventually, all structures distal to the constriction are reduced to an avascular cord. The connection between the toe and the foot becomes increasingly tenuous, and if not surgically amputated, the toe spontaneously detaches without bleeding. Autoamputation typically occurs within five years. Cole described four stages of ainhum: Grade I: Formation of the groove. Grade II: Ulceration of the groove's floor. Grade III: Involvement of the bone. Grade IV: Autoamputation. Pain is a common symptom, reported in approximately 78% of cases. Mild pain is present in the early stages due to pressure on underlying nerves. Severe pain may occur with phalangeal fractures or chronic sepsis. Histological examination reveals changes in the prickle cell layer, leading to the deposition of condensed keratin that forms the groove. The junctional tissue is reduced to a slender, almost avascular fibrous thread. Beyond the constricting band, tissues are replaced by a fibro-fatty mass covered with hyperkeratotic skin. Radiological findings in the early stages include soft tissue constriction on the medial aspect of the fifth toe and distal swelling. In Grade III lesions, osteolysis is observed near the proximal interphalangeal joint, often with a tapering effect. Dispersal of the head of the proximal phalanx is common. After autoamputation, the base of the proximal phalanx typically remains. Radiological imaging is crucial for early diagnosis and staging, which can help prevent amputation. Ainhum must be differentiated from congenital annular constrictions and other conditions such as leprosy, diabetic gangrene, syringomyelia, scleroderma, and Vohwinkel syndrome. Treatment options vary depending on the stage of the disease. Simple incisions across the groove are ineffective. In Grade I and II lesions, excision of the groove followed by Z-plasty can relieve pain and prevent autoamputation. Grade III lesions are managed by disarticulating the metatarsophalangeal joint, which alleviates pain and preserves a functional and stable foot.
